篳篥可在日本雅樂（gagaku）中聽見，是雅樂兩個主要旋律樂器之一，也用於日本神: The hichiriki can be heard in Japanese gagaku; it is one of the two main melodic instruments of gagaku and is also used at Shinto weddings. It appears in all the forms of gagaku except the recitation of poetry, and its development is bound up with the decline in Japan of the popularity of tōgaku (Tang music). In these settings it is heard with its loud double-reed tone. Japanese players such as Hideki Togi are worth hearing, as is playing by Thomas Piercy, along with Aneesh Kashalikar's audio-visual demonstration.
篳篥屬氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號422.111.2，以竹或木: The hichiriki is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 422.111.2, with a tube of bamboo or wood, a double reed of cane or wheat straw at the top, and played end-blown. Its line can be traced back to the Chinese bili, which reached Japan in the Tang period; scholars hold that it took its present form after the twelfth century, in step with the decline of what was then called Tang music in Japan. The hichiriki is also related to the Korean piri, and its fingering notation uses signs derived from Chinese characters. In gagaku it serves as one of the main melodic instruments, and it appears at Shinto weddings and on like occasions.
篳篥屬氣鳴樂器，發聲體為雙簧。來源記載管身以竹或木製成，也有資料具體說以一段竹材: The hichiriki is an aerophone whose sounding body is a double reed. The sources record a tube of bamboo or wood, and one source says specifically a length of bamboo; a flat double reed of cane or wheat straw is set into the top. The tube is bored with holes and played end-blown. Beyond bamboo, wood, cane and wheat straw the sources state no materials for the other parts, so none are guessed at here.
篳篥是一種帶有獨特穿透力的管樂器，其音色明亮刺激，具有強烈的個性特徵。音質帶有輕: The hichiriki is a wind instrument with a distinctive penetration; its timbre is bright and arresting and its character strong. The tone has a slight nasality and an old, weathered quality — neither warm nor fully dark, but with a sharpness of its own. Its range sits in the upper middle register, and it controls volume well enough to stand out clearly in an ensemble. Its resonance rests on the fine vibration of the reed, and with the narrow, long tube this produces its characteristic penetration. Compared with the clear brightness of the dizi, the hichiriki has more of a bleak quality; compared with the roundaboutness of the xiao it is more direct and forceful. In the traditional music of East Asia the hichiriki often leads, and its particular sound sets off the solemn, archaic atmosphere of a piece.
篳篥為雙簧氣鳴樂器，管身開洞，採豎吹方式。演奏時將頂端扁平雙簧含入口中，以口風控: The hichiriki is a double-reed aerophone with a bored tube, played end-blown. The player takes the flat double reed at the top into the mouth and controls pitch and ornaments — slides above all — with the embouchure; the technique of sliding the pitch is the first thing a beginner must learn. Because of the double reed, tone and intonation are hard to keep steady, so a beginner practises taking the reed, blowing and shaping the embouchure before going on to slides. The source gives no details of holding position or fingering.
篳篥（Hichiriki）為日本雙簧木管樂器，屬氣鳴類，霍恩博斯特尔–薩克斯編號: The hichiriki is a Japanese double-reed woodwind, an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 422.111.2. The tube is bamboo or wood, with a reed of cane or wheat straw at the top, bored with holes and played end-blown; the bore is cylindrical, pitch and ornaments are controlled mainly by the embouchure, and the instrument is known for its slides. It developed from the Chinese bili, is related to the Korean piri, and is one of the main melodic instruments of Japanese gagaku; it is also common at Shinto weddings.
